title: A field experiment on the effectiveness of spiders and carabid beetles as biocontrol agents in soybean
location: University of Kentucky Spindletop Research Farm, Fayette County, Kentucky, USA
design: RBD with 3 blocks differing in distance from field edge; 6 plots total (three 7x7 m spider-carabid reduction plots enclosed by 36-cm aluminum flashing with 5-cm inward-facing ledges, and three unmanipulated unfenced control plots); spiders removed daily-to-biweekly by pitfall traps and hand searching; carabids excluded by fencing but not actively removed; soybeans (var. Essex) planted in rows 0.9 m apart; no insecticides; 1994 growing season.
notes: This is an EXCLUSION/REDUCTION experiment: spiders were actively removed and carabid immigration was blocked by fencing. The treatment successfully reduced spider and carabid densities by ~75% (spiders ~4-fold lower in reduction plots; carabids ~75% lower activity-density). Despite this large reduction in generalist predators, yield did NOT decrease — it was marginally HIGHER in predator-reduction plots (P=0.064), opposite to the expected biocontrol direction. No herbivore group was more abundant in predator-reduction plots. The paper concludes the trophic cascade from spiders/carabids to soybean yield was too weak to detect, possibly due to low ambient pest densities, intraguild predation, or simply a weak link between predators and yield. Weed differences (fewer weeds in frequently disturbed fenced plots) may explain the marginally higher yield. Plant height, pods per plant, and average seed weight did not differ between treatments (P > 0.35). Yield unit is kg dry beans per 7x7m (49 m2) plot.

observations.treatment_description: spider-carabid reduction: fenced 7x7 m plots with 36-cm aluminum flashing + 5-cm inward ledges; spiders removed daily to biweekly by dry pitfall traps and hand searching of vegetation; carabid immigration blocked by fencing
observations.control_description: unmanipulated unfenced 7x7 m plots with natural spider and carabid beetle populations

figure_read.located_by: caption search on page 4: 'Soybean production, measured as kg of beans harvested per plot'
figure_read.structure: Two bars side by side: filled/black = Control, open/white = Spider-Carabid Reduction; y-axis 'Weight (kg)/ plot'; ticks at 0, 10, 20; spacing 10; linear; (*) symbol near bars indicates P < 0.10; error bars are ± SE (paper convention: ± SE throughout, Table 1 states ± SEM).
figure_read.evidence_note: Fig 2 p4; open/white bar (Spider-Carabid Reduction); bar top sits about 40% between 10 and 20 ticks (~14 kg/plot); error bar cap extends to ~17, SE ~3. Control (filled/black bar): bar top approximately at the 10 tick (~10 kg/plot), error bar cap ~12, SE ~2. DIRECTION OPPOSITE TO EXPECTED: predator-reduction plots yielded marginally MORE than controls (F1,2=14.1, P=0.064). Assignment re-checked: legend clearly marks filled=Control, open=Reduction. Paper discusses this at length — attributes to fewer weeds in fenced plots due to more frequent disturbance. The apparent increase in yield with predator reduction was NOT statistically significant.

observations.unit: mean number per shake-cloth sample (bean leaf beetles, Cerotoma trifurcata)
observations.data_source: text, Results section PDF page 5; values stated: 'Mean numbers per sample for control and spider-carabid reduction treatments, were, respectively, 17.7 ± 3.2 and 14.5 ± 4.0 for bean leaf beetle (F1,2 = 2.30, P = 0.27)'
observations.notes: Shake-cloth method: single 1-m section of soybean row per plot, August and September dates. Values are means per sample. Variance for treatment arm: SE = 4.0; for control arm: SE = 3.2. Not significant (F1,2=2.30, P=0.27). Direction: pest numbers were NOT higher in predator-reduction plots — slightly LOWER, opposite expected for herbivore release. Paper reports bean leaf beetle density was slightly above economic injury level in the first sampling but well below it in the second sampling when spiders and carabids were most abundant.

observations.unit: mean number per shake-cloth sample (Lepidoptera larvae)
observations.data_source: text, Results section PDF page 5; values stated: '9.8 ± 1.9 and 8.3 ± 1.2 for Lepidoptera larvae (F1,2 = 3.86, P = 0.188)'
observations.notes: Shake-cloth method: same sampling as bean leaf beetle. Variance for treatment arm: SE = 1.2; for control arm: SE = 1.9. Not significant (F1,2=3.86, P=0.188). Lepidoptera larvae densities were below economic injury levels throughout the experiment. Direction: pest numbers were NOT higher in predator-reduction plots — slightly lower, opposite expected.
